formulas.derivation: 1000/pi = 318.31, simplified to 318. So n = Vc * 318 / D

videos.title: YOUR FEEDRATE IS WRONG! - Haas Automation Tip of the Day

formulas.name: Effective Feed Rate Compensation (circular interpolation)

F_desired.description: Desired effective feed rate at cutting edge

formulas.notes: Use this whenever milling circular pockets or thread milling. For thread milling, replace D_hole with major thread diameter.

formulas.name: Feed Rate Amplification Factor

amplification.description: How many times faster the edge moves vs programmed center

formulas.notes: When tool is nearly the same size as the hole, amplification can be 10x or more.

formulas.name: Toolpath Diameter

D_toolpath.description: Diameter of the circle the tool center follows

formulas.notes: This is the circle the CNC programs the feed rate for. The outer edge (actual cut) is D_hole.

example_calculation.notes: 550/50 = 11x amplification. To get F30 at the edge, program F2.73 at centerline.

tribal_tips: Programmed feed rate is at the CENTERLINE of the tool, not at the cutting edge
When milling circular pockets with a tool nearly the same size as the hole, effective feed rate can be 10x higher than programmed
This is the most common cause of bad surface finish in circular pocket milling
Solution 1 (preferred): Use CAM system arc feed rate compensation (e.g., Mastercam has this built in)
Solution 2: Calculate manually using F_program = F_desired * (D_hole - D_tool) / D_hole
Solution 3: Use cutter compensation (G41/G42) with tool diameter in offset page - control auto-compensates in tight corners via Setting 44
This problem is worst when thread milling - thread mill moves much faster at edge than centerline
For thread milling: replace hole diameter with major thread diameter in the formula
Most CAM systems handle this automatically when you let them calculate toolpaths
If hand programming to part contour with cutter comp, enter exact tool diameter on offset page

videos.title: Spindle Speed Variation (SSV) - Stop Chatter on Your CNC Lathe - Haas Automation

formulas.name: SSV RPM Range
formulas.formula: RPM_high = RPM_commanded + Setting_165; RPM_low = RPM_commanded - Setting_165

formulas.name: SSV Cycle Period

T_cycle.description: Time for one complete SSV cycle

formulas.notes: Each unit of Setting 166 equals 0.1 seconds

Setting_165.name: SSV Spindle Speed Variation
Setting_165.description: Controls how many RPM above and below commanded speed the spindle will vary
Setting_165.effect: At 150, spindle varies +/- 150 RPM from commanded speed (total 300 RPM range)

Setting_166.name: SSV Variation Cycle Rate
Setting_166.description: Controls how fast the spindle cycles through the RPM variation
Setting_166.effect: At 12, one complete RPM sweep takes 1.2 seconds

with_ssv.result: Much better finish at same diameter where chatter occurred
with_ssv.notes: SSV prevented chatter escalation even at 6:1 L/D ratio

extreme_test.result: No chatter with SSV and decent finish even at 20:1 L/D with tail stock

tribal_tips: SSV = Spindle Speed Variation - continuously varies RPM to prevent chatter resonance from building
Chatter is a self-reinforcing resonance: rough surface -> more vibration -> rougher surface -> more vibration
SSV breaks the resonance cycle by spending very little time at any single RPM
Available on ALL Haas lathes - use M38 to turn ON, M39 to turn OFF
Setting 165 controls RPM swing (how much variation), Setting 166 controls cycle time (how fast it varies)
SSV is most effective for: boring, turning long shafts, grooving, any operation prone to chatter
Start with moderate values: Setting 165 = 100-200 RPM, Setting 166 = 10-15
SSV works best when chatter is moderate - extreme chatter from terrible setups may still have some chatter
SSV can extend your capabilities: turn thinner/longer parts without tail stock support
The ST-30 cut so well under normal conditions it was hard to force chatter - SSV is preventive, not just corrective
Typical L/D ratios: under 4:1 usually fine, 4:1 to 6:1 may need SSV, above 6:1 usually needs tail stock + SSV
With SSV, achieved 20:1 L/D ratio in 1040 steel with decent finish - normally impossible without special tooling
Tool geometry matters: larger nose radius + slow feed rate = more time in cut = more chatter tendency
SSV does NOT affect programmed feed rate - only spindle speed varies

consolidated_tips: SPEED vs RPM: 'Speed' (SFM/Vc) is the linear velocity at the cutting edge. RPM is rotational speed. Same SFM requires different RPM for different diameters.
The tractor tire analogy: A small tire and large tire traveling at the same ground speed have the same SFM, but the small tire spins at higher RPM.
Always get cutting speed (SFM/Vc) from the specific tool manufacturer's catalog, not generic tables - coatings can double allowable speeds.
Know your material: ISO groups (P/M/K/N/S/H) are universal, but the sub-number varies by tool manufacturer.
4140 steel example: Kennametal P4, Sandvik P2.1, Niagara/Seco P5, Iscar P6/P7 - same material, different vendor numbering.
When catalog gives a range (e.g., 200-300 SFM), more rigid setup = use higher end, longer tool = use lower end.
Tools live longer at slower cutting speeds - there is always a tool life vs productivity trade-off.
Programmed feed rate is at tool CENTERLINE, not cutting edge - critical for circular pocket milling and thread milling.
When tool diameter approaches hole diameter, effective feed at edge can be 10x+ higher than programmed - compensate or you'll get terrible finish.
Preferred compensation method: Let CAM system handle arc feed rates (Mastercam, etc.). Manual method: F_prog = F_desired * (D_hole - D_tool) / D_hole.
Haas NGC control has built-in calculator: Current Commands > Calculator tab with Tapping, Milling, Turning, Drilling tabs.
SSV (Spindle Speed Variation) is the primary tool for fighting chatter on Haas lathes - M38 ON, M39 OFF.
SSV works by preventing resonance from building - spindle never stays at one RPM long enough for chatter to escalate.
SSV Settings: Setting 165 = RPM variation amount, Setting 166 = cycle time (units of 0.1 sec).
Starting SSV values: Setting 165 = 100-200 RPM variation, Setting 166 = 10-15 (1.0-1.5 seconds per cycle).
SSV achieved 20:1 L/D ratio turning in 1040 steel with decent finish - normally requires special tooling or steady rest.
Chatter is self-reinforcing: rough cut -> vibration -> rougher cut -> more vibration. SSV breaks this cycle.
SSV does NOT change feed rate - only spindle speed varies. Feed rate stays as programmed.
Cutter compensation (G41/G42) with tool diameter in offset page + Setting 44 allows the control to auto-compensate feed rates in tight corners.
Round RPM values for cleaner programs (3056 -> 3100) - exact decimal RPM is unnecessary.
